title: Delhi HC Refuses to Recall Order Cutting NHAI Concessionaire's ₹911 Crore Termination Payment
meta_description: Delhi High Court let stand its order striking down the ₹911 crore termination payment component of KEPL's arbitral award against NHAI.
bench: Bench composition not confirmed in available reporting
case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. M/s Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited
citation: 2026:DHC:5961 (as reported); order dated 28 September 2026 declining to disturb the order dated 28 July 2026
body: Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited, a special purpose vehicle floated by Kalpataru Projects International, built and ran a stretch of national highway under a concession from the National Highways Authority of India. NHAI terminated that concession in 2021. KEPL took the dispute to arbitration and, on 16 August 2024, walked away with two awards in its favour, the larger of which turned on what NHAI owed as a termination payment.

The tribunal fixed that termination payment at Rs 911.13 crore, working from a 'Total Project Cost' of Rs 1045.5 crore that NHAI itself had notified through a disaggregation letter. NHAI's own contract put a ceiling on this head of claim. Article 48.1 of the concession agreement capped the termination payment at Rs 650 crore. The gap between the contractual cap and the sum the tribunal actually awarded became the heart of NHAI's challenge.

NHAI took that challenge to the Delhi High Court under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the standard route to resist an award on narrow grounds such as patent illegality or conflict with the fundamental policy of Indian law. A court hearing a Section 34 petition is not meant to re-weigh evidence or substitute its own view of the facts for the tribunal's. It can only step in where the award crosses one of a short list of statutory lines, and a contractual cap written into the concession agreement, exceeded without a basis the contract itself recognises, is exactly the kind of thing that can tip an award into that territory.

On 28 July 2026 the Court gave NHAI partial relief. It set aside the part of the award covering the termination payment and the interest running on it, while leaving every other head of the award, including KEPL's other claims, undisturbed. That split outcome is itself telling. The Court was not persuaded that the tribunal's entire process was flawed, only that one specific computation, the one that produced a number nearly forty percent above the contractual ceiling, could not stand.

KEPL did not accept that outcome quietly. It asked the same court to reconsider, and on 28 September 2026 the Court declined. The order of 28 July stayed exactly as it was: the termination payment component remains set aside, and the rest of the award remains intact. Kalpataru Projects International told the stock exchanges the next day that the Delhi High Court had upheld its earlier order.

For KEPL, this is a loss on the single largest number in its claim, even though it keeps whatever the tribunal gave it under the other heads. The company has not treated the matter as closed. Its exchange filing says it believes it has a strong case and is taking further legal steps, including filing a petition, language that points toward an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act rather than acceptance of the result.

The case sits inside a now familiar pattern on Delhi's commercial roll, where NHAI concession terminations from the pandemic years keep generating large awards that courts are willing to pare down specifically where a tribunal's arithmetic runs past a cap the parties wrote into their own contract. A tribunal can read a disaggregation letter generously. It cannot use that letter to override a ceiling the concession agreement fixed in black and white, and once a High Court takes that view at the Section 34 stage, a second attempt to reopen it before the same court was always going to be an uphill climb.

What happens next matters for every concessionaire sitting on an NHAI termination payment claim still working its way through arbitration. Model concession agreements in the highway sector carry the same kind of contractual ceiling that undid KEPL's larger claim, and tribunals asked to compute a termination payment from a disaggregation letter or similar correspondence will now have a fresh reminder that the ceiling, not the correspondence, has the last word. A Section 37 appeal, if KEPL files one, would go to a Division Bench and would have to grapple with the same narrow standard of interference that already decided the matter once, which is a demanding brief even for a well-resourced litigant.
why_it_matters: Concessionaires suing NHAI for termination payments should not assume a tribunal's own cost computation survives court scrutiny intact. Where a concession agreement fixes a hard ceiling on this head of claim, as most NHAI model agreements do, an award that exceeds it through a generous reading of ancillary correspondence is vulnerable at the Section 34 stage, and a reconsideration application before the same bench is unlikely to succeed once that view has been taken.
card_summary: Delhi HC refused to recall its order cutting the termination payment component of KEPL's award against NHAI, holding the ₹911 crore figure exceeded the ₹650 crore cap fixed in the concession agreement.
card_tip: Check your concession agreement's termination payment ceiling before relying on a tribunal's cost computation to survive a Section 34 challenge.
verification_notes: Two orders (28 July 2026 and 28 September 2026) and the underlying award figures (Rs 911.13 crore termination payment vs Rs 650 crore Article 48.1 cap, Rs 1045.5 crore Total Project Cost) are confirmed across PSU Connect, Verdictum (which cites the neutral citation 2026:DHC:5961), S&A Law Offices' Legal 500 update, Sahi.com and KEPL's own NSE/BSE corporate disclosures dated 29 July and 29 September 2026. The exact bench (judge's name) was not confirmed in the reporting reviewed and is left out rather than guessed. The precise nature of KEPL's further legal recourse (an appeal under Section 37 versus another remedy) is described only in general terms in the company's own filing, so the article does not assert a specific forum beyond what the filing says.
